part.text: {"type":"finish","output":"Technical analysis of the queue incident between 09:00 and 09:46 using only synthetic evidence E01 through E10. The incident is best explained as an external rate-limiting event in dependency B that triggered cascading amplification inside the worker pipeline. At 09:00 the system was healthy: queue depth of 120 and eight workers indicate normal load with comfortable headroom. By 09:10 queue depth had grown more than fifteen-fold to 1,850 with no change in worker count, which is inconsistent with organic user-driven load growth on a 9-minute timescale given the steady baseline minutes earlier. E10 explicitly rules out deploys, schema changes, host restarts, route changes, and credential rotations, so the surge is not attributable to internal change management. E05 shows that dependency B began returning HTTP 429 for 31% of requests at 09:15, E06 shows retry volume increasing by 420% under an exponential-backoff policy capped at three retries, E07 shows that doubling workers from 8 to 16 reduced queue depth by only 6% in ten minutes, E08 shows that disabling retries for dependency B dropped queue depth 38% in six minutes while direct failures rose, and E09 shows that once dependency B lifted its rate limits the queue returned below 150 in eleven minutes. Taken together, dependency B rate limiting is the primary cause; the retry policy and fixed worker pool are amplifiers. The retry policy is particularly damaging because exponential backoff multiplies concurrent in-flight requests during the first attempt wave, which worsens 429 pressure on the upstream dependency and creates a feedback loop in which each retry increases the probability of further throttling. This explains why the retry storm was self-reinforcing and why simply adding workers provided almost no relief: workers consume throughput that dependency B has already constrained, so additional workers cannot drain a queue whose bottleneck is an external 429 ceiling. The fact that disabling retries for dependency B reduced queue depth 38% in six minutes while raising direct failures is the cleanest causal evidence in the dataset, because the only behavior changed was the retry amplification mechanism. E04 indicates resource utilization remained moderate at 09:14, with CPU 43%, memory 51%, and disk 22%, which further argues against host saturation as the primary driver. Recommendations therefore focus on adaptive retry behavior, admission control at the dependency boundary, worker elasticity tied to upstream capacity rather than queue depth alone, and explicit rate-limit awareness. Uncertainties remain around whether dependency B raised limits voluntarily or after escalation, whether other dependencies experienced softer throttling, and the precise distribution of task types hitting B. A plausible alternative hypothesis is that an organic traffic spike caused the surge, but E10 rules out configuration changes and E09 shows recovery coinciding with B's limit raise, not with any local capacity change, which weakens that hypothesis. Another alternative is host resource exhaustion, but E04 contradicts it.
